cards.title: The Only Professional
cards.instruction: Behave as the only qualified person present. Correct mistakes with patient, increasingly strained professionalism.

cards.title: Can You Keep It?
cards.instruction: Use increasingly sensitive details to test whether someone deserves deeper trust.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: The club menu changes next month. Keep that out of the committee chat; I'm checking who I can brief.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'll just tell Sam. He helps me with the ordering.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: No forwarding through useful people. The chef has resigned. Can you keep that out of an order form?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'll order the usual quantities. Nobody needs a reason from me.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Good. I accepted her resignation because I'm taking over the kitchen. Please let me tell Sam that myself.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 tests menu discretion; A3 corrects B2's Sam exception and supplies a chef resignation; A5 entrusts A's takeover after B4 demonstrates an operational way to keep quiet.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 useful-colleague exception causes A3's no-forwarding correction. B4 offers ordinary ordering without explanation, which makes A5's deeper personal disclosure a response to discretion.

relationship.evidence: B2 wants Sam informed for ordering rather than gossip alone; B4 adapts helpfully to A's correction without becoming an impossible secrecy machine.

heightening.evidence: A5's personal takeover is more sensitive than A3 resignation and A1 menu, so B4's answer changes actual information access.

specificity.evidence: A1 club menu, B2 ordering work, A3 departing chef and A5 takeover form one intelligible kitchen change.

brevityWit.evidence: A3's useful-people correction addresses B2's rationale. A5's Sam instruction protects the new disclosure instead of explaining the trust test.
